Spread across the building, the works create something closer to a temporary, darkly dreamt habitat than a conventional white-cube exhibition. Most have never been exhibited. Håstad mounted a small, four-work presentation at Carl Kostyál in Stockholm in 2016, the year that gives this decade-long survey its starting point. By the time Håstad arrives and we sit down in the backyard, the building is beginning to fill for a friends-and-family evening. His father, the poet and literary critic Kristoffer Leandoer, has just arrived. Håstad knows people are waiting for him, but the conversation is focused. He drinks water from a champagne glass. He has spoken publicly in recent years about sobriety, and there is little sense here of hiding behind the Yung Lean persona. We are speaking primarily to Jonatan, though, as he points out, he does not find the distinction especially useful. “I’m Jonatan. I created Yung Lean, and I also made all of these artworks,” Håstad told Artsy. “So I think it all belongs together.” He does, however, see one important difference. His visual work remains less trained and therefore less professionalized. “I like the rawness,” he said. Years of touring taught him exactly where to stand and how a show should sound. “Sometimes you become too pro.” In fact, the visual side came first. Håstad calls graffiti his “first big love,” an obsession from around the age of 11 or 12. As a child, he would also spend hours drawing and carving small figures from wood. Music never displaced that instinct. Even while producers were still finishing tracks, he recalls, his mind would already be moving toward the music video: the clothes, the lighting, the image around the song. That visual practice has since expanded into film and acting, including a role in the forthcoming Netflix film Sacrifice , the recent “STORM” video, and a contribution to the soundtrack for the upcoming video game Grand Theft Auto VI . “The visual side has always been very important to me,” he said. “Visual art came first, and then music came afterward.” The rawness Håstad describes permeates the exhibition. Figures emerge from blunt fields of color; alien-eyed faces and checkerboards recur from work to work. The large paintings can feel provisional even when densely populated, with passages of drawing, paint, pattern, and empty ground allowed to coexist. A glazed ceramic such as El Jefe (2022) turns the same vocabulary into a lumpy, comic body. In Perfekt Dejt (Perfect Date) (2025), two figures recline amid a dark, highly saturated forest. That uncanny, slightly unreal atmosphere extends through the building. Music, low light, and daylight slip through half-open windows and move across its exposed industrial walls. A miniature diorama and a separate TV room deepen the sense that Håstad has temporarily occupied the space rather than simply hung work inside it. Håstad says he became more willing to take risks around 2016, moving among acrylic, oils, oil sticks, ceramics, and video and beginning to work at larger scales. Asked what changed, he is succinct: “I worry less. I care less about what other people think.” He has never attended art school. His formal training amounts to a two-week clay course at Folkuniversitetet, a Swedish adult-education organization. This is not a deficit he is eager to correct. “I think there’s something really beautiful about someone who has a job, like, if you’re a plumber, and on the side you make little wooden sculptures,” he said. His music developed through years of practice until it became his profession. “But this isn’t my job, and I want to keep it pure.” The exhibition nevertheless marks an unmistakable new stage in Håstad’s relationship with the art world. A selection of works, primarily sculptures, will later be sold through the auction house Bukowskis. He sees no contradiction. Håstad has no gallerist and no external curator, and much of the exhibition has been assembled with people he has known since school. His longtime friend Kaj Lindhé Gimdal has helped with both Håstad’s process and the show’s curation; Håstad also shared a painting studio for roughly three years with Benjamin Reichwald , better known as the rapper Bladee. “If I went to Bukowskis and saw that Robert De Niro had painted a picture, I’d still want to buy it because Robert De Niro painted it,” Håstad said. “In my case it’s always going to be, ‘Yung Lean made this.’ There’s no getting around that. And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that at all.” For Håstad, the model echoes the way his music career began. “I entered the music world without a record label or management,” he said. “We just uploaded things online, and it was a bit of a ‘fuck you’ to the music industry.” Some 15 years later, he wants to approach art in much the same way: rent the space, finance it himself, build it himself, then work with an established institution such as Bukowskis where it serves a purpose. That willingness to engage with the art market does not extend to how Håstad wants the exhibition itself to function. Almost none of the works have been shown publicly before, and admission is free. “One thing I find boring about the art world is that everything is so gatekept,” he said. “It’s only for rich people, or only for people who are already inside the scene.” His own celebrity, he argues, makes openness more important, not less. “I’m a fucking famous musician. So, of course this should be open to everyone. It should be free to enter and open for a long time.” Even visitors who cannot afford an artwork should be able to leave with something small, he said, whether a calendar or a key. “Everyone should be able to take something away with them.” That independence also informs Slåtter . Håstad traces the film to a soldier’s cottage his mother inherited in Småland, and to childhood encounters with the strange, sometimes frightening imaginative world of Swedish nature. He cites the work of illustrators John Bauer and Elsa Beskow , as well as folklore around mythological trolls Näcken and the invisible spirit Vittra . “That whole Swedish troll forest becomes very real when you’re a child,” he said. “Then you get older, and you understand what reality is. Somewhere in there, I think I just wanted to get that feeling back in a film.” As Håstad talks about Bauer’s troll forests and Nordic figures, I mention that Slåtter made me think of Ali Abbasi’s Border (2018). It is, unsurprisingly, a film Håstad admires. He praises the way it places the bureaucratic realities of border control and policing alongside something magical. Stockholm itself becomes another subject of our conversation. Having lived abroad for many years, I tell Håstad that the city can feel strangely inert despite its beauty, unless you have access to the right social or creative contexts. He partly agrees. The team had discussed staging the exhibition in London or Paris before deciding against it. “But fuck it. I’m from Stockholm,” he said. “Stockholm made me, and Stockholm is where I want to give something like this back.” If the exhibition encourages younger artists to find a room of their own, put on shows or concerts, and remain “a little naïve” rather than immediately seeking entry into an established market, he said, “that would be fucking amazing.” It is a fitting ambition for an exhibition that, viewed from Barnhusbron, looks anything but tentative. Håstad may want to preserve the amateur freedom of making art, but after a decade of doing so largely outside public view, he is no longer keeping it hidden.

title: How Madonna Became an Art World Icon
summary: Madonna, 1990 Patrick Demarchelier Staley-Wise Gallery The legend is a classic one: A 20-year-old Michigan college dropout lands in New York with $35 in her pocket and gets into a taxi for the first time in her life, telling the driver to drop her off at “the center of it all.” Soon, the ambitious young Midwesterner would dye her hair blond and find herself at the center of the city’s creative scene. She would date Jean-Michel Basquiat , become close friends with Keith Haring , hang out with Larry Gagosian , collect Frida Kahlo works, and pose for Maripol . Somewhere along the way, she would also become the most famous singer in the world, known simply by her first name: Madonna . On the eve of the 43rd Video Music Awards, where Madonna leads this year’s field with 11 nominations, Artsy looks back at the Queen of Pop’s unusually deep ties to the art world—and the artists, images, and ideas that have shaped her career. A muse in the downtown scene Madonna, NYC, 1980, 1980 Mick Rock Avant Gallery The center of it all during Madonna’s meteoric rise in the 1980s was her small but tightly knit downtown community. Living in a fifth-floor walk-up in Alphabet City, she quickly absorbed the neighborhood’s feverish creative output and became a fixture at now-legendary venues including Danceteria and the Roxy. A Panel of Experts, 1982 Jean-Michel Basquiat Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO) It was within this milieu that perhaps the most valuable artwork featuring Madonna emerged, painted by her then-boyfriend Jean-Michel Basquiat. A Panel of Experts (1982), a largely black-and-white work in acrylic and oil pastel, bears Madonna’s name in its upper-left corner alongside that of Basquiat’s ex-girlfriend Suzanne Mallouk . At its center, two chunky figures appear to be fighting—an apparent reference to an altercation between the two women over Basquiat. Now in the permanent collection of the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts , the painting was reunited with its muse decades later when Madonna posed in front of it during its inclusion in the Barbican’s 2017 exhibition “Basquiat: Boom for Real.” Making the Madonna image Madonna (True Blue), 1986 Herb Ritts CAMERA WORK "Madonna at Window, NYC 1986", 1986 Herb Ritts Izzy Gallery If Madonna became one of the defining faces of 1980s pop culture, photographers and stylists helped fix that face in the collective imagination: ripped fishnets, heaps of bracelets, bleached hair, thick eyebrows, and a gaze that could turn provocation into a dare. Her largely DIY style fascinated photographers including Herb Ritts and Patrick Demarchelier , but some of the era’s most intimate images came through the lens of Maripol, the French-born photographer, stylist, and downtown fixture who also helped construct the bridal-inflected look of Madonna’s Like a Virgin era. Madonna (First Single), 1983 Maripol Exploring the Arts Benefit Auction A 2017 solo exhibition of Maripol’s work at Dundee Contemporary Arts captured Madonna on the brink of global takeover. The disarming Polaroids show an icon before the mythology had fully hardened: Madonna in bed in 1983; Madonna trying on a pink wig backstage in 1984. They are images of a superstar in formation. The downtown language of street art Eric Kroll - Madonna at Danceteria, NYC 1983 Memorial for Michael Stewart, 1983 Eric Kroll Alpha 137 Gallery Madonna also had unusually early access to graffiti and street art through her relationships with Basquiat and Haring. During the years when Haring was painting murals at era-defining nightclubs such as the Palladium and Danceteria, Madonna was performing at many of the same venues, trying to make early hits such as “Holiday” and “Everybody” heard. When her first major nationwide concert run, the Virgin Tour, wrapped in 1985, she held its after-party at the Palladium, with her friend’s work looming in the background. That friendship was inseparable from activism. As HIV/AIDS was met with intense stigma and governmental neglect, Madonna became an outspoken supporter of AIDS research and fundraising. She frequently appeared at benefit events alongside Haring and other members of their downtown circle, including Kenny Scharf . Madonna, 2009 Mr. Brainwash Rago/Wright/LAMA/Toomey & Co. Keith Haring Andy Warhol record cover art (after Keith Haring Andy Warhol Madonna), ca. 1986 Keith Haring, Andy Warhol Lot 180 Gallery Decades later, she returned to the visual language of street art for the cover of her 2009 greatest-hits album Celebration , for which Mr. Brainwash transformed her image into a brightly colored, stencil-like portrait. The Pop palette inevitably evokes Andy Warhol , another figure in Madonna’s orbit and a guest at her 1985 wedding to Sean Penn. Warhol and Haring even collaborated on a wedding gift for the couple: four works that transformed New York Post covers about the publication of Madonna’s nude photographs into playful Pop art artifacts. The tabloid image, already central to Madonna’s career, became an art object. The collector behind the pop star Madonna’s relationship with art was not confined to the people around her. Long before she could afford to collect it, she was looking. As a teenager, she encountered Frida Kahlo through black-and-white photographs at the Detroit Institute of Arts. She later recalled walking past the museum’s Diego Rivera murals to look at images of Kahlo in her studio, captivated by the Mexican artist’s “self-possession and unique beauty.” During her first month in New York, with money still scarce, Madonna spent part of her budget on a postcard of Kahlo’s Self-Portrait with Monkey (1940), which she came to regard as a kind of “guardian angel.” Frida Kahlo, 1931 Imogen Cunningham Atlas Gallery Picasso, 1932 (printed 1981) Man Ray L’SPACE Gallery Years later, the actual painting became hers. Madonna acquired Self-Portrait with Monkey at auction in the late 1980s and loaned it to Tate Modern for its 2001 Kahlo survey. Around a decade later, she deepened her holdings with another of Kahlo’s most visceral works, My Birth (1932), acquired through a private sale. It is easy to see what Madonna found in Kahlo: an artist who fashioned autobiography, physicality, sexuality, and pain into an uncompromising public image. Those same forces have run through Madonna’s own career, which has repeatedly tested the standards imposed on women’s bodies and turned sexuality into both spectacle and a means of self-authorship. Kahlo is far from the only modernist in Madonna’s collection . Works by Pablo Picasso , Fernand Léger , Man Ray , and Tamara de Lempicka have also been reported among her holdings. From collector to collaborator Madonna’s engagement with art has never stopped at ownership. Over the decades, she has maintained an unusually active network of friendships, collaborations, and partnerships with living artists. The forms of that support vary considerably. In 1997, she sponsored MoMA ’s exhibition “ Cindy Sherman : The Complete Untitled Film Stills.” In 2001, she presented the Turner Prize to Martin Creed during a live broadcast. And in 2017, she joined Brooklyn Museum director Anne Pasternak and artist Marilyn Minter for a public discussion about feminism and art. Minter is also represented in Madonna’s collection, as is Tracey Emin . Madonna owns Emin’s 2001 mixed-media work It Just Happens , a characteristically unguarded declaration of desire and autonomy, qualities that readily rhyme with Madonna’s own creative persona. Madonna : Time lapse photograph spiritual value, 1998 David LaChapelle Eternity Gallery Her relationships with artists continue to evolve. During a visit last year to Emin’s foundation in Margate, England, Madonna met with young artists in residence—and did not leave empty-handed. Works she encountered there, including sculptures by Brazilian artist Anderson Asteclines and a small painting by Ethiopian artist Kirubel Mandefro, now hang in her London townhouse. The gesture says something about the kind of collector Madonna has become. Her interest is not restricted to trophies by canonical names. The same curiosity that once drew her toward artists in downtown New York still appears to guide her toward work being made now. When art becomes material For another pop star, name-checking an artist in a lyric or borrowing an artwork for a stage set might read as cultural signaling. With Madonna, the relationship is harder to separate from the work itself. She did not observe the downtown culture that produced Basquiat, Haring, Scharf, and Julian Schnabel from a distance. She emerged from inside it. In that sense, Madonna was not simply a muse to artists. She adopted one of their fundamental strategies: treating the self as material. Her body, clothes, sexuality, religion, celebrity, and public image became things to be constructed, dismantled, quoted, and reconstructed again. Art history consequently surfaces throughout her career almost as a second visual language. Horst P. Horst ’s photographs famously informed the video for “Vogue,” while the imagery surrounding “Open Your Heart” drew heavily on the paintings of de Lempicka. Minter’s Green Pink Caviar (2009) became a video backdrop on Madonna’s Sticky & Sweet Tour, while animated versions of Haring’s radiant figures appeared elsewhere in the show. Helen Bennett, Cape, 1936 Horst P. Horst Robert Klein Gallery Femme a la Mandoline, circa 1933 Tamara de Lempicka Heritage Auctions More recently, the references have migrated into the lyrics themselves. On 2012’s “I Fucked Up,” Madonna imagines an unrealized domestic future: “We coulda bought a house with a swimming pool / Filled it up with Warhols, it would be so cool.” But perhaps no song makes the relationship between Madonna and the art world as explicit as her recent single “Danceteria.” Released this summer, the track looks back at the scene from which she emerged, name-checking Haring, Basquiat, Maripol, Fab Five Freddy , Scharf, and powerful downtown dealer Tony Shafrazi. It plays almost like an oral history set to a dance beat. More than four decades after Madonna arrived in New York asking to be taken to “the center of it all,” “Danceteria” makes the case that she did not simply find that center. She was part of what made it one.

title: Brazilian artist Lucia Laguna dies at 85.
summary: Brazilian painter Lucia Laguna , whose densely layered landscapes transformed the view from her Rio de Janeiro studio, has died at 85. She was one of the country’s most celebrated and distinctive contemporary artists. Laguna died Sunday at her home in Rio de Janeiro, according to her gallery, Fortes D’Aloia & Gabriel , which represented her for two decades. “Throughout her career, Lucia developed a body of work defined by her engagement with landscape, memory, and everyday life,” the gallery said in a statement. “Her work, at once intimate and open to the world, occupies a fundamental place in contemporary Brazilian art.” The gallery closed its São Paulo space for a day in her memory, and in memory of Rodrigo Cass , another artist on its roster who recently died in an accident. Laguna came to painting late, by an unusual route. Born in 1941 in Campos dos Goytacazes, in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro state, she spent three decades teaching Portuguese and Latin language and literature at public schools before enrolling, in the mid-1990s, at the Escola de Artes Visuais do Parque Lage in Rio. There, under the mentorship of Charles Watson, who taught creativity research, she began developing the practice that occupied the rest of her life. Her first solo exhibition in Brazil opened in 1998 at the Cândido Mendes Cultural Centre in Rio. It quickly drew attention to her work. Her 2012 inclusion in the 30th Bienal de São Paulo marked what is widely considered the turning point that established her as one of the country’s leading contemporary artists. Laguna’s paintings drew on what was immediately around her: the gardens, houses, fences, and power lines visible from the windows of her home and studio in Rio’s northern suburbs, where she lived and worked for more than 40 years. The artist divided her output into a set of recurring series—“Paisagem” (Landscape), “Jardim” (Garden),” “Estúdio” (Studio),” “Pequenos Formatos” (Small Formats), and, more recently, “Azulejo” (Tiles) — through which she repeatedly returned to and reworked the same fragments of city and foliage. Laguna built up her compositions through an unusual collaborative process. Assistants and art students spent weeks covering a canvas in acrylic paint and pictorial motifs, a practice described as a kind of visual conversation. Then Laguna took over, dividing the surface with masking tape into fields, lines, and angles, then reworking it in oil over multiple rotations. The result was a technique of accumulation and erasure, with forms appearing and dissolving across successive layers. That approach earned Laguna a string of honors in Brazil, including the CNI-SESI Marcantonio Vilaça prize for the visual arts in 2006–07 and the PIPA Prize, jointly awarded by the PIPA Foundation and Rio’s Museu de Arte Moderna, in both 2011 and 2015. Her work entered major Brazilian public collections, including MAM São Paulo , MAM Rio , MASP, Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR) , the Museu Nacional in Brasília, and the Centro Cultural São Paulo. Internationally, she had solo exhibitions in 2019 at Cologne’s Galerie Karsten Greve (who showed her work in Europe), and in 2022 at London’s Sadie Coles HQ, where her show was titled “Life Is Only Possible Reinvented.” MASP staged a solo presentation of her work, “Vizinhança,” in 2018. In her final years, Laguna’s work underwent a marked shift after she left the home and garden that had anchored her practice for four decades. She relocated roughly three years ago to an apartment in Rio’s Laranjeiras neighborhood, a denser, more urban area between two mountains in the city’s southern zone. The move brought her closer to her canvases and to her new neighbors, and pushed her compositions toward more fractured, semi-abstracted views obscured and framed by windows, doors, and tiles. That transition was the subject of her 2025 exhibition “ A Propósito de Duas Janelas ” (Regarding Two Windows) at Fortes D'Aloia & Gabriel in São Paulo. It was her fourth show with the gallery and was accompanied by an essay from critic and curator Diego Matos. This past May, Laguna opened her first solo exhibition in the United States, “ Apenas Meus Cabelos São Brancos ” (Only My Hair Is White), at the New York gallery Galerie Lelong , organized in collaboration with Fortes D’Aloia & Gabriel. The show, which ran through June 27, 2026, and included a walkthrough led by curator Larry Ossei-Mensah , presented new paintings from her “Pequenos Formatos” and “Paisagem” series. The windows of the artist’s Laranjeiras studio were both subject and compositional device. Laguna is survived by her daughter, Laura, and her grandchildren, João and Daniel. In their statement, Fortes D’Aloia & Gabriel extended condolences “to her family and friends, and all those who had the privilege of knowing Lucia and her work.”

title: The Met to stage major Felix Gonzales-Torres exhibition in summer 2027.
summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art will stage the first major New York survey of Felix Gonzalez-Torres 's work since 1995, opening in summer 2027. “ Felix Gonzalez-Torres: The Spaces Between ,” on view June 10th through October 18th, 2027, will present more than 40 works by the Cuban-born American visual artist encompassing installation, painting, photography, sculpture, and video, drawn from public and private collections. Included in the exhibition will be defining works such as, "Untitled" (Go-Go Dancing Platform) (1991) which consists of an empty blue platform ringed with 48 lightbulbs that is briefly activated once per day by a lamé-clad go-go dancer; "Untitled" (Perfect Lovers) (1987–1990), twin battery-powered clocks which are initially set to the same time and slowly desynchronize; and "Untitled" (Revenge) (1991) a continuously replenished pile of blue candies in clear wrappers. Rather than a conventional monographic show, the exhibition will place works within the Museum’s permanent collection galleries, ranging from Egyptian art and medieval art to historic British interiors. “Felix Gonzalez-Torres is one of the most important artists of the 20th century. His installations transform ephemeral materials into enduring experiences that grapple with ideas such as time, loss, and love,” said Max Hollein, the Met's director and CEO. “For the first presentation of the artist in New York City in over three decades, the Met will showcase his art throughout the museum, in conversation with 5,000 years of human creativity.” Untitled, 1994 Felix Gonzalez-Torres Carolina Nitsch Contemporary Art The exhibition is organized in collaboration with the Art Institute of Chicago , which will mount a simultaneous, distinct exhibition, “This Work Cannot Be Destroyed.” David Breslin, curator of modern and contemporary Art, who organized the show with curator Ann Goldstein, described Gonzalez-Torres's work as inseparable from the crisis that shaped it. “The AIDS crisis was the crucible that forged his resolute conceptual clarity, and his brilliance was creating an open-ended body of work where new meanings can be embedded into historical ones,” Breslin said. Goldstein, who is now interim director of the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles, co-organized the artist's first major survey in 1994. Three decades after his death, she remarked that the work remains “simultaneously deceptively beautiful and rigorously acute, defiantly romantic and precisely analytical—and uncannily present.” The exhibition's title is drawn from a 1994 fax Gonzalez-Torres sent his friend and gallerist Andrea Rosen, quoting the poet Elizabeth Bishop, “I watched closely the spaces between the birds.” Born in Guáimaro, Cuba, in 1957, Gonzalez-Torres left the country as a child, living briefly in Spain and then Puerto Rico before settling in New York in 1979. He attended the Whitney Independent Study Program and earned his BFA from the Pratt Institute, and from 1987 to 1994 was a member of Group Material, the politically engaged artists' collective co-founded by Doug Ashford , Julie Ault , and Tim Rollins . His best-known works invite viewers to physically deplete them, taking a candy from a seemingly endless pile, or a sheet from a towering stack of paper, turning gallerygoers into collaborators in works about circulation, loss, and the boundary between public and private life. He died of AIDS-related complications in 1996, at 38. Interest in Gonzalez-Torres’s work has surged this year. A large survey at the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid, “Dulce Venganza” (“Sweet Revenge”), co-curated by Nancy Spector and Alejandro Cesarco, gathers more than 50 works through October 12th and has drawn attention for how directly the artist’s warnings about “encroaching conservative forces in government,” as Spector has put it, resonate today. In February, the Fundación Fernando Romero staged an exhibition at Mexico City's La Cuadra San Cristóbal, the Luis Barragán –designed house, pairing Gonzalez-Torres’s beaded curtains, mirrors, and light strings with Barragán’s architecture in what curators called “a poetic dialogue” between two artists who never met. Gonzalez-Torres himself pointed to art's transformative power in his own writing. Describing a visit to see Roni Horn ’s Gold Field (1982) with his partner, Ross Laycock, as Laycock was dying of AIDS-related illness, he wrote that the work was “a new landscape, a possible horizon, a place of rest and absolute beauty.” An accompanying catalogue will include newly commissioned texts by Breslin, Goldstein, Paulina Pobocha of the Art Institute of Chicago, and Samuel Shapiro of the Met. Gonzalez-Torres described his intentions simply, “Above all else, it is about leaving a mark that I existed: I was here. I was hungry. I was defeated. I was happy. I was sad. I was in love. I was afraid. I was hopeful. I had an idea and I had a good purpose and that's why I made works of art.”

title: Painter Emily Mae Smith's Surreal Visions Embrace the Dark Side
summary: Painter Emily Mae Smith believes that in dark times, it’s best to embrace the shadows. Last week, the artist—best known for her surrealistic paintings of anthropomorphized broomsticks—opened “ Transit of Venus ” at Petzel Gallery . It’s her first solo exhibition in New York in over four years, on view through October 24, 2026. The anticipated show brings together 15 new oil paintings and two carved benches made from 2023 to 2026. The works range in scale from the handheld to the monumental and embrace a dizzying range of formal strategies. Smith reprises her saucy broomsticks, revels in hyperrealism , and takes inspiration from French agrarian tableaux. These varied works are united by Smith’s use of deep shadow and how she sees that shadow in relationship to painting. In the canvas Becoming Neolithic (2026), one of the first works Smith conceptualized while building the show, a towering thicket looms over snowy ground. Hands emerge from its stalks with seeking gestures, reaching toward the sky. The scene is backlit by a setting winter sun. In the foreground, a fox treads over the shadowed snow. It’s one of many paintings in the show that positions the viewer in a place of darkness. Becoming Neolithic, 2026 Emily Mae Smith Petzel Gallery Midnight Assembly, 2023-2026 Emily Mae Smith Petzel Gallery “Culturally, we’re in the shadow,” Smith said as she walked through the show ahead of its opening last week. “We’re in a Jungian shadow-reveal sort of space as a society,” where “repressed desires become desperate grabs of power.” She feels a sense of obligation to explore this territory. “Whether or not we want to go there, it’s there. We have to explore it,” she said. “Painting the light from behind is a way of saying: I am the dark side of the image—I’m working from the other side.” In the years since “ Heretic Lace ,” Smith’s last exhibition with Petzel in 2022, the artist has relocated from New York City to the Hudson Valley. She now works in a studio in Kingston, New York, where she feels more connected than ever to her natural environment. At the same time, she feels throttled by the pitch of U.S. political upheavals and speed of visual consumption through social media. In another new painting, Only Human (2026), a bunch of grapes appear in translucent, noxious hues of purple, green, blue, and red. Inside each grape is a human eyeball, sloshing in turbulent water. The grape motif (which reappears in Shadow Land Zeuxis , (2026)) references a classical story about the conflation of reality and illusion. Smith’s painting is simultaneously funny and disturbing and visualizes the pressures of the attention economy, resulting in a frantic, superficial, and distracted mode of existence, with eyes unsure where to turn. In these times, Smith believes painting can, at the very least, offer a sense of orientation. The exhibition title “Transit of Venus” refers to a rare astronomical event in which the planet Venus passes directly between the Sun and Earth. The planet appears as a small dark spot moving across the face of the solar disk. These transits occur in pairs eight years apart, with more than a century separating each pair. Historically, astronomers used the transit of Venus to calculate the distance between Earth and the Sun. These measurements helped establish the scale of the solar system—and, essentially, our understanding of our place in the universe. Smith’s paintings formally reflect this idea. “Venus moves across in front of the Sun and becomes a little black dot. That effect connects to the use of backlighting in my work and the way we can know ourselves by seeing something moving in front of us,” she explained. For the artist, it’s essential to imagine ourselves as bodies in motion, to embrace transformation amid rising authoritarianism in the U.S. “Trying to stay unfixed is a purposeful way to resist the painful transformation we’re having in society right now,” she said. “Being unfixed is dangerous, and people want to eliminate it.” For Smith, the “Venus” of the exhibition title refers equally to the Roman goddess, herself an adaptation of Aphrodite, and a historical embodiment of this embrace of ambiguity and multiplicity. “Venus was used by different people, for different reasons, across time and history,” the artist said. Smith’s anthropomorphized broomsticks have long served as a nod to the historic position of women in the arts, a winking reference to feminine labor and the male gaze. In this exhibition, Smith’s most iconic motif loosens and morphs, at times, into a Venus-like figure. She sees her painting Becoming Neolithic as an adaptation of the broomstick, as well as The Locust II (2026), which reimagines the 1872 painting The Grasshopper (La Cigale) by French painter Jules Joseph Lefebvre . While Lefebvre renders his nubile young woman as helpless, cowering, naked, and alone, Smith gives her a broomstick and a scythe that serve as a protective weapons. In the painting Venus (Inner Vision) (2026) meanwhile, Smith makes the handle of her torso-like broomstick translucent. The figure’s organs—brain, liver, stomach—and circulatory system are visible, like a version of the “anatomical Venuses” created in 18th-century Florence, wax visions of idealized young women used to teach anatomy. “I wanted to take the idea of a Venus and literally give her interiority,” said the artist. In these paintings, translucency aids in Smith’s attempt to reenchant people with the magic of painting. “I wish people would consider what it takes to make a painting, and how painting can exist in the world in a complex, fabulous, magical way, and not just as trading cards on the internet, or auction-house commodities,” she said. “So there’s this desire to see inside and make that beautiful.” Understanding the materiality of painting, she thinks, might be one way to do that. In Sacred Conversation (2026), Smith brings together the animals and plants whose materials become the tools of painting—from badger and sable hair used in brushes to walnut oil, flax, cotton, and cuttlefish-derived sepia. The imagined ecosystem of creatures that could never coexist in nature becomes a kind of portrait of painting itself and its entanglement with the natural world. The structure of the painting, meanwhile, riffs on paintings by Giovanni Bellini and the Renaissance tradition of the sacra conversazione, the gathering of saints. It is a moment of bright light among shadows. Smith believes that we are living through a moment of societal transformation whose repercussions are still coming into view. “In my last show, I was really interested in my place in painting as a person, as a woman painter, in my own time—how do I belong, what are the problems of trying to belong inside this thing,” Smith said. “Now, I’m asking, what is a painting to the world right now, when it all feels like it’s on fire?” One of the final works completed for the show, The Changeling (2026), depicts a foot held aloft against the dark sky. It transforms from flesh to straw, and a hand reaches toward it with a lit match, like an inverse of Michelangelo ’s Creation of Adam (ca. 1512) . Flames are imminent. But they also bring much-needed illumination.

title: Photographer Tyler Mitchell awarded $250,000 Crystal Bridges prize.
summary: Photographer Tyler Mitchell has been awarded the $250,000 Don Tyson Prize for the Advancement of American Art by the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art . Mitchell is the sixth recipient of the prize, and the first to receive it under its new terms. Founded in 2016 as a biennial $200,000 award, the Don Tyson Prize is now awarded as an annual award with an increased purse. The unrestricted cash prize, established by the Tyson family in honor of the late Don Tyson, former chairman and CEO of Tyson Foods, recognizes individuals and institutions working in any medium whose work changes how the public looks at, thinks about, or experiences American art. “Our selection of Tyler Mitchell reflects the profound impact of his practice and the distinctive place his work holds in contemporary culture,” said Rod Bigelow, executive director of Crystal Bridges. “Through photography, film, publishing, fashion, and exhibition-making, Mitchell has created images and experiences that reach audiences well beyond traditional museum spaces.” Olivia Tyson, president of the Tyson Family Foundation and granddaughter of Don Tyson, added that Mitchell "reflects the spirit of the Don Tyson Prize: bold, generous, forward-looking, and culturally consequential. His work offers a powerful vision of life, beauty, leisure, and belonging." Mitchell, born in Atlanta in 1995 and now based in Brooklyn, received a BFA in film and television from NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts in 2017. He made history the following year as the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of American Vogue , with a portrait of Beyoncé for the magazine’s September 2018 issue. His photography, film, and installation work is defined by a portrayal of Black life centered on tenderness, camaraderie, and self-determination, often drawing on the pastoral landscapes and domestic scenes of his suburban Georgia childhood. Artsy named Mitchell one of the most influential artists of 2025, and he is represented by Gagosian . Deborah Willis , a mentor to Mitchell who received the Don Tyson Prize in 2022, said of his work: “Tyler captures the diversity and commonality of a community by activating memories of childhood, family, and leisure that form the fabric of social and cultural life. Tyler’s work re-frames perceptions of intimacy, style and the human form.” Long before the Vogue cover, Mitchell traced his interest in photography to skateboarding in Atlanta, where he began shooting photos and videos of friends. “You begin to just tell people you're a photographer until it actually happens,” he said in a 2016 interview with Lomography , describing how the habit snowballed into a practice. He has said he resists being defined solely as a fashion photographer, despite frequent commercial and editorial work with brands including Marc Jacobs, Givenchy, and Converse. “I have been using clothes to tell stories in my photography," he told Lomography, contrasting his approach with work that "uses photography to tell stories about clothing,” which he called “extremely boring.” The Don Tyson Prize has previously gone to Nicholas Galanin (2024), Willis (2022), Project Row Houses (2020), vanessa german (2018), and the Archives of American Art (2016). Crystal Bridges was founded in 2005 by philanthropist Alice Walton and opened in Bentonville, Arkansas, in 2011.

title: MSCHF transforms two Lexus electrified vehicles into surreal sculptures.
summary: MSCHF , the Brooklyn-based conceptual art collective represented by Perrotin , will debut a pair of surreal new car sculptures in New York this week as part of a collaboration with Lexus. The works reconfigure two of the automaker's electrified vehicles for the exhibition “Motomorphosis,” which opens this week at Chelsea Industrial during Armory Week. The show pairs each unaltered vehicle with its distorted double. A Lexus RZ450e appears once as itself and again as Circle Car , looped nose-to-tail into an endless, driving circle, while a Lexus RX450h+ is shown alongside Twisted Car , its body pulled into dramatic longitudinal torsion. MSCHF describes the works as “Form Cars,’ positioned as an inversion of the automotive industry’s "Concept Car" prototypes. Kevin Wiesner, the collective's chief creative officer and a founding member, told Highsnobiety the project drew on the vocabulary of 3D animation, where forms bend and stretch without being fixed, as well as on a lineage of car-as-medium artworks in the United States, such as Pippa Garner' s sculpture and performance Backwards Car (1974). “We had the idea of inverting the Concept Car and taking a purely Formalist approach to the object,” Wiesner said. Despite their seemingly impossible shapes, the sculptures were built using conventional auto-body techniques—a steel armature built up with thousands of individual pieces, then finished with the paint and Bondo overcoat typical of a body shop. Some components, Wiesner said, are actual Lexus parts, "but they're sculptures, not cars." Lexus has framed the collaboration around what it calls "Electric Made Art," treating electrification itself as an artistic medium rather than a purely functional one. "Most conversations about electrification focus on how a vehicle is powered. ‘Motomorphosis’ asks a different question: what can electricity power in our imagination?" said Lisa McQueen, Lexus's senior manager of marketing. "Working with MSCHF allowed us to take the automobile beyond its familiar form and explore movement, transformation and possibility in an entirely new way." “Motomorphosis” will have a public opening the evening of Thursday, September 24th, and will be on view Friday, September 25th, and Saturday, September 26th.

title: Musician Solange Knowles to debut her first public large-scale sculpture.
summary: Grammy-winning musician and artist Solange Knowles will debut her first public large-scale sculpture at an exhibition organized by Google Chrome on New York’s High Line later this week. The work will be unveiled as part of “Unfinished Projects,” an exhibition running September 24th through 27th at the High Line ’s Chelsea Market Passage in New York, alongside a companion online digital experience. Chrome invited Knowles, along with musician PinkPantheress and NFL quarterback Joe Burrow, to bring an unfinished idea to life and share their process, framing the project around how “the right tools can help move a stalled idea forward.” Knowles has described her sculpture as an examination of “how we process space and structure,” aimed at breaking down the barrier between artist and audience. She used the Google Chrome web browser to research the work, organize its production, and finalize the logistics of bringing it to life. The piece will be shown in progress rather than complete, giving visitors a look at her process alongside the two other, similarly unfinished commissions. The sculpture marks a new medium for Knowles, though the singer has long been interested in large-scale sculpture. In an excerpt from Living With Chamberlain , a volume on the sculptor and filmmaker John Chamberlain published by Assouline, Knowles described encountering his work for the first time at the Chinati Foundation in Marfa, Texas, around 2008 or 2009, calling it a “visceral response.” In a conversation with Rainer Judd for Interview magazine , she said she recognized her own process in Chamberlain’s crushed-metal forms. “I maximize and then minimize. I saw his sculpture, and I felt like there was a synergy,” she said. She traced the same instinct to her curatorial and musical work more broadly, describing it as a “maximalist-minimalist” approach of gathering wide before narrowing to a single form, and said she sought out Chamberlain’s sculptures in museum collections as she traveled, including at Houston’s Menil Collection and Museum of Fine Arts. Knowles has built a substantial performance and visual-art practice alongside her music career. She founded the creative agency and archive Saint Heron in 2013 and has staged performance pieces at the Guggenheim Museum in New York (2017), the Chinati Foundation (2017), and the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg (2019). In 2019, she closed the 58th Venice Biennale with a performance exploring protection, transformation, and spiritual passage. Her 2018 interdisciplinary piece “ Metatronia ” featured Metatron's Cube , a sculpture she conceived and built, staged at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles. That same year, an extended director‘s cut of her film When I Get Home screened at institutions including the Los Angeles County Museum of Art , the Brooklyn Museum , and the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. She was also named the Harvard Foundation’s Artist of the Year and composed a score for the New York City Ballet—only the second woman of color to do so. Knowles’s practice has increasingly centered on programming. In 2019, the artist programmed a curated series of performances and films titled “Bridge-s” at the Getty Center in Los Angeles, presented with Dropbox and IAMSOUND, including new choreography by Gerard & Kelly alongside films by Julie Dash, Jenn Nkiru, and Nuotama Bodomo, and an original score performed with musician Cooper-Moore. “Bridge-s is a reflection on how much transition can be controlled and accelerated by our own ideas, thoughts, and movements vs. the natural process of time and space,” Knowles said in a statement at the time. Her forthcoming sculpture for “Unfinished Projects” sits at the nexus of these interests in large-scale production, curating, public programming, and artwork that evolves in real time.

title: 9 Artists Who Shaped Korea’s Dansaekhwa Movement
summary: Blue-Umber ‘76, 1976 Yun Hyong-keun PKM Gallery In mid-20th-century South Korea, amid the economic hardship and political repression that followed the Korean War, a vanguard of abstract artists forged a radical new visual language. Pushing back against rigid, state-sanctioned academic realism and breaking decisively from centuries of traditional fine-art ink painting, these artists sought an art form untethered from past conventions. The Korean art critic Lee Yil curated a selection of their works into a groundbreaking group show at Tokyo Gallery in 1975; he coined the term Dansaekhwa in 1980 to define these nonfigurative works executed in understated, neutral hues. Though the term translates to “monochrome painting,” the label is a misnomer. Dansaekhwa was never about the passive application of a single color. Rather than treating the canvas as a flat window for representation, these artists rejected Western compositional logic altogether, elevating process over final result and prioritizing physical labor as a form of spiritual meditation. Through disciplined repetition—dragging gouges through wet paint, soaking and tearing traditional Hanji paper, or squeezing pigment through coarse hemp from behind, for example—they rendered the physical surface an arena of endurance and material transformation. Meditation 91007, 1991 Chung Chang-Sup Axel Vervoordt Gallery Over the past decade, a surge of international retrospectives, such as the 2015 “Dansaekhwa” exhibition at the 56th Venice Biennale (curated by art historian Yongwoo Lee) and major market interest, have cemented Dansaekhwa as one of modern art history’s vital movements. This November, Phaidon will publish Dansaekhwa: Korean Abstract Art and Its Cultural Impact by Dr. Yeon Shim Chung, the first major study of its kind. As the international art world recalibrates following another bustling edition of Frieze Seoul , global attention remains fixed on South Korea’s rich modern art legacy . Driven by landmark gallery retrospectives and major international surveys, from Venice to San Francisco and Seoul, Dansaekhwa continues to stand out as the defining cornerstone of Korean abstraction. The following nine artists offer essential entry points to the movement. Kim Whanki B. 1913, Kijwa-do, Korea. D. 1974. 26-I-70, 1970 Kim Whanki San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) Heaven and Earth 24-IX-73 #320, 1973 Kim Whanki Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art Pioneering modernist painter Kim Whanki is revered as the foundational precursor to Dansaekhwa. He was active between Seoul, Paris, and New York throughout his long and transformative career. Kim primarily worked on monumental oil canvases, filling his expansive surfaces with tens of thousands of small blue dots enclosed within tight, hand-drawn square grids. These sweeping abstract compositions, rendered in translucent washes of indigo, navy, and oceanic teal, evoke vast starry night skies or shimmering water as they bridge traditional Korean nature motifs (mountains, moon jars, and sky painting specifically) with Western modernism. The watery, ink-like transparency of his oil pigment creates a deeply atmospheric, meditative depth that immediately sets his work apart from American field painters. By translating spiritual harmony into systematic markmaking, Kim laid the ideological groundwork for the generation of Korean abstract artists that followed. Today, the artist holds an unrivaled position at the apex of the Korean art market, setting a historic auction record in 2019 when his painting 05-IV-71 #200 (Universe) (1971) sold for over $10 million and became the most expensive artwork ever by a Korean artist. His monumental legacy is preserved at the dedicated Whanki Museum in Seoul, while key works anchor the permanent collections of major institutions such as the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA), Korea , and the Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art . Kwon Young-Woo B. 1926, Riwon, Korea. D. 2013 Kwon Young-Woo was a Paris- and Seoul-based master who abandoned traditional ink brushes early in his career and worked with paper as a sculptural medium. Kwon used his fingers, fingernails, wooden tools, and scratch awls to tear, puncture, scratch, and layer multiple sheets of white hanji paper. His medium-to-large-scale monochromatic compositions feature rhythmic, torn incisions and subtle three-dimensional relief, occasionally accented by soft blurs of blue or dark ink seeping through from the reverse side. The resulting works resemble delicate, highly tactile topographies; the physical destruction of the paper becomes the generative act of creation. Kwon forced a radical reevaluation of paper’s role in Korean and broader East Asian art history, bringing it into a modern context. His work was featured in the benchmark survey exhibition “Dansaekhwa” at the 56th Venice Biennale in 2015. Today, his tactile paper compositions are preserved in the permanent collections of major global institutions, including the MMCA in Seoul, the British Museum in London, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris. Chung Chang-Sup B. 1927, Cheongju, Korea. D. 2011 Seoul-based painter and longtime academic Chung Chang-Sup spent decades investigating the raw, organic possibilities of tak , the natural mulberry bark fiber used to craft traditional Korean Hanji paper. Foregoing conventional oil paint, Chung soaked raw mulberry fibers in water, kneaded the wet pulp by hand, and pressed it directly onto large canvas stretchers. As the pulp dried, it formed surface cracks, fibrous ridges, and subtle folds that revealed the medium’s organic origins. His finished works present thick, sculptural surfaces in muted, earthy monochromatic tones of ivory, warm tan, charcoal, and slate gray. They often feature squares and rectilinear shapes embedded in their centers. Chung viewed his labor-intensive process as unifying his own breath and physical effort with the natural material. His tactile approach to material heritage gained global prominence when he was featured in the historic collateral exhibition Dansaekhwa at the Palazzo Contarini-Polignac during the 56th Venice Biennale in 2015. His works are now held in renowned international collections, including the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York, the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) in Korea, the Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art, and M+ in Hong Kong. Yun Hyoung-Keun B. 1928, Cheongju, Korea. D. 2007 Yun Hyoung-Keun was a Seoul-based artist who produced some of the most emotionally resonant and understated works of the Dansaekhwa movement. Working on large, unprimed linen and raw cotton canvases, Yun applied wide, vertical bands of dark, heavily diluted oil paint using a signature mixture of burnt umber and ultramarine pigment. These towering dark pillars feature soft, feathery borders where the watery paint bleeds naturally into the untreated fabric, creating deep, gate-like architectural voids of near-black alongside raw cloth. The resulting paintings feel monumental yet remarkably quiet, visually echoing the natural bleeding of traditional ink wash on absorbent paper. Informed by personal trauma during Korea’s post-war political turmoil (he went to prison and was nearly executed for participating in student movements), Yun’s work treated canvas as an acoustic chamber for grief and restraint. His international stature was solidified by a landmark posthumous solo retrospective at Palazzo Fortuny during the 58th Venice Biennale in 2019 . His market momentum continues this September with a solo exhibition at PKM Gallery in Seoul, accompanying the historic restoration and public opening of his longtime residence and studio in the city. New York’s Judd Foundation will also open a solo show of his work on October 8th. Yun’s oeuvre is represented in major permanent collections worldwide, including the MMCA in Korea, Glenstone in Maryland, and Tate Britain . Park Seo-Bo B. 1931, Korea. D. 2023 Park Seo-Bo is recognized as the father of Dansaekhwa. He served as the movement’s theorist and organizing force, championing Korean art from his perch in Seoul until his passing. He is most famous for his lifelong “Écriture” series (1972–2023): In the 1980s, Park developed a technique of soaking sheets of traditional Hanji (mulberry paper) for weeks, layering it onto canvas, and pushing the wet pulp with his fingers, sticks, and rulers to build abstract, sculptural ridges, often referred to as Hanji “mountains.” The artist’s early palette was restricted to unbleached white, inspired by the translucent purity of Korean Joseon porcelain, and deep matte black, recalling the soot lining traditional Korean kitchen hearths. Beginning in the early 2000s, Park introduced luminous hues drawn directly from nature, naming specific shades such as Maple Leaf Red, Canola Yellow, and Sky Gray. Park saw this relentless, daily repetition as an exercise in self-erasure and spiritual healing for both the artist and the viewer. Seoul’s Kukje Gallery is currently celebrating his legacy with a retrospective that remains on view through October 18th. His footprint continues to expand with the recent opening of the Park Seo-Bo Memorial Museum in Seoul, alongside key acquisitions by prestigious institutions like Tate Modern in London, the Museum of Modern Art in New York, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris. Chung Sang-Hwa B. 1932, Korea. D. 2025 Untitled 019-5-2, 2019 Chung Sang Hwa Gallery Hyundai Chung Sang-Hwa , who worked between Paris, Japan, and South Korea, was an internationally celebrated artist who approached painting as a labor-intensive ritual of construction and deconstruction. He coated large canvases with a thick mixture of kaolin clay and acrylic paste, let them dry, then methodically folded them into tight, uniform grid patterns. The rigid surfaces cracked, clay peeled away, and the artist refilled the empty geometric voids with oil paint. Repeating this painstaking cycle dozens of times produced subtle, mosaic-like surfaces of off-whites, grays, or muted blues with intricate textural depth. Up close, Chung’s canvases reveal a complex relief of tile-like fragments that catch ambient room light. In 2021, Seoul’s National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) honored the artist with a sweeping solo retrospective. His works are permanently housed in major institutional collections across the globe, including the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C., M+ in Hong Kong, and the MMCA in Korea. Ha Chong-Hyun B. 1935, Korea. Conjunction 23-67, 2023 Ha Chong-hyun Tina Kim Gallery Seoul-based master Ha Chong-Hyun has revolutionized the physical mechanics of canvas painting through his long-running “Conjunction” series. The artist eschews traditional front-facing brushwork, instead applying thick, muted oil paint in shades of taupe, dark ocher, rust brown, and charcoal to the back of coarse burlap or hemp fabric. Using significant physical force, he squeezes the viscous pigment forward through the open weave of the fabric until it oozes out the front, where he scrapes, smears, or shapes the paint using trowels and palette knives. The final works feature heavy, sculptural impasto trails protruding from rough, unpainted burlap. Ha’s unconventional technique turned painting inside out, transforming coarse industrial sacking into a tactile battlefield. His work reached milestone prominence in 2022, when Kukje Art and Culture Foundation organized a solo show at Fondazione Bevilacqua La Masa as an official Collateral Event at the 59th Venice Biennale . On September 25th, the artist will open a major presentation at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco: his first-ever North American retrospective. His pieces form an integral part of major permanent collections around the world, including MoMA and the Guggenheim Museum in New York, as well as the Centre Pompidou in Paris. Lee Ufan B. 1936, Kyongnam, South Korea. From Line, 1974 Lee Ufan Upsilon Gallery Lee Ufan is an internationally renowned painter, sculptor, and philosopher who splits his practice between Japan, France, and South Korea. Lee occupies a unique position in art history: while recognized as the key theoretical architect of Japan’s Mono-ha ( School of Things ) movement in the late 1960s, he simultaneously served as a vital international bridge for Dansaekhwa. Though scholars debate the artist’s exact categorization—his “Relatum” series of spare sculptures align with Mono-ha’s prioritization of physical, unmediated interactions between raw industrial materials and natural objects, while his rhythmic paintings share more with Dansaekhwa—Lee’s practice links both movements via a philosophical commitment to restraint and material dialogue. To make his famous “From Point and From Line” series, Lee holds his breath for up to two minutes, synchronizing his body with his brushwork: His deliberate strokes of mineral pigment fade systematically across bare canvas. Lee remains the most commercially successful living Korean artist, with benchmark works like East Winds (1984) achieving over 3.1 billion won ($2.7 million) at auction in 2021. His institutional footprint is secured by dedicated foundation spaces in Naoshima, Japan, Arles, France, and Busan, high-profile site-specific commissions at the Château de Versailles and the Hirshhorn Museum , and a retrospective organized by the Dia Art Foundation at SMAC Venice as an official Collateral Event of the 61st Venice Biennale this past year. Lee Dong-Youb B. 1946. D. 2013 Interspace, 2008 Lee Dong-Youb The Columns Gallery Interspace, 1980 Lee Dong-Youb The Columns Gallery Lee Dong-Youb represents the younger wave of artists associated with Dansaekhwa's initial push; he was included in Lee Yil’s seminal 1975 exhibition “Korea: Five Artists, Five Hinsek ‘White’” in Tokyo. The Seoul-based artist studied under Lee Ufan and was celebrated for his radically spare visual language. Lee’s signature “In-Between” series consists of expansive canvases covered in ultra-thin, translucent layers of pale white and soft gray paint. Applied with broad, whisper-light brushstrokes, his quiet gradations of tone leave vast, cloud-like central spaces that evoke open sky, architectural light, and infinite silence. The subtle shifts between pale pigment and bare canvas are so delicate that they require slow, contemplative viewing to register. By stripping painting down to its most minimal atmospheric presence, Lee pushed monochrome abstraction to its logical extreme. The artist launched into prominence after winning the Grand Prize at the 1972 Seoul National Exhibition, establishing the second-generation trajectory of Korean monochrome abstraction. Today, his understated works are held in premier museum collections, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA) in Gwacheon, the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo (MOMAT), and the Seoul Museum of Art (SeMA). Browse more artworks by Dansaekhwa masters on Artsy.

title: All the Art You Need to See During Armory Week 2026
summary: Each September in New York after Labor Day, the art world returns from a much-needed summer break and dives headfirst into a bounty of gallery openings, art fairs, and major museum shows. This year, though, the city’s fall fairs— The Armory Show and Independent 20th Century —have shifted their dates back, gifting us a reprieve. Instead of cramming everything into one whirlwind week, the season’s newness unfolds across the month, with a little more headspace to take in all the art. That doesn’t mean September has been quiet. The month has already brought several sprints of gallery openings and a few major museum shows, with some of the fall’s biggest exhibitions still on the horizon. Now, with fair week upon us, it’s the perfect moment to catch up: hit the fairs, pop by galleries, and see what’s newly opened across the city. While you’re at it, it’s the perfect time to make a res at one of the city’s new art-forward restaurants, which we rounded up here . Nearly all are close to the venues listed below. We’ve spent the past few weeks making the rounds. Here’s our 10-stop guide to the art to see during Armory Week 2026. 1. The Armory Show Sep. 24–27 | Javits Center, 429 11th Ave | Hudson Yards The Armory Show returns with its usual mix of international galleries, small and large, plus curated sections that keep things interesting ( around 230 exhibitors are taking part this year). I suggest starting with Presents, the section for younger galleries, and Solo, with its single-artist presentations ranging from historical 20th-century names to emerging talents. Both Focus, curated by María Elena Ortiz, and Platform, dedicated to large-scale works, spotlight artists of the Caribbean and its diaspora. The fair is doing plenty of programming, including Armory Live, a multiday series of talks, many featuring artists. And new this year is Armory After Hours, an evening event on Friday, September 25th, from 7 to 9 p.m., where you can explore the fair and experience a processional performance inspired by Caribbean carnival led by DJ and creative producer Adam “Foreigner” Cooper. 2. Independent 20th Century Sep. 24–27 | The Breuer, 945 Madison Ave | Upper East Side Independent 20th Century moves uptown this year to perhaps its most fitting venue yet: the Breuer building, now Sotheby’s headquarters . It’s an apt setting for the fair, which is less concerned with the century’s known quantities than its lesser-known artists and artworks. Several presentations even revisit artists who once showed in the building during its years as the Whitney , the Met Breuer , and the Frick . This edition brings 57 exhibitors, most presenting solo or two-person shows. Highlights include the Andy Warhol Foundation ’s presentation of the artist’s little-known homoerotic drawings; and several galleries will spotlight women of Abstract Expressionism , including Olney Gleason , Berry Campbell , and Bueno & Co. 3. The Guggenheim 1071 Fifth Ave | Upper East Side The Guggenheim just opened a major new show: Taryn Simon ’s “ Father Country I Do Love You ,” which takes over the entire rotunda. Nearly a decade in the making, the show spans 42 works, including photography, video, sculpture, and many, many stories, built around the real life of an unnamed federal agent—whose career touched everything from fingerprinting Jodie Foster to 9/11. Simon shares stories from his time on the job and connects them with bigger questions of power and politics. The show is on view through March 14, 2027. While uptown, I recommend a quick stop at some nearby galleries: Danh Vō at White Cube , Thea Djordjadze at Sprüth Magers , and Bea Scaccia at Gagosian (which opens September 22nd). 4. Chelsea Gallery Shows Chelsea Before or after Armory, head south to take in Chelsea’s standout shows. Three I would recommend are: Anthony McCall at Sean Kelly : You have to experience McCall’s light installations in person to begin to understand their magic. The show spans his landmark early work, Line Describing a Cone (1973), through to a new installation. Sara Anstis at Olney Gleason : Anstis ’s tiny, intricate pastels are oh so delectable. She draws on mythology, medieval imagery, folklore, and Old Master painting, but the works are inarguably entirely her own—filled with mysterious ladies, skinny dogs, and dreamlike scenarios. Eric N. Mack at Paula Cooper : In “ You Red the Shirt Off My Back ,” Mack presents fabric-based installations and sculptures that translate the language of painting into three dimensions, while also bringing art and fashion into conversation. 5. Tribeca Gallery Shows Tribeca No New York art week is complete without a trip to Tribeca, arguably the city’s most interesting gallery hub. Here are three shows worth stopping by: Melissa Joseph at Charles Moffett : “Casserole Culture” brings together 15 new works exemplifying Joseph’s mesmerizing capacity to “paint” with wool. Ranging from small sculptures with found objects to massive needle-felted paintings, the works delve into the artist’s personal experiences, family, and upbringing. Edith Dekyndt at Marian Goodman : “ Notes on What Is What ,” her first show since joining the gallery’s roster, incorporates video, installations, and drawing to explore and surface imperceptible elements of the everyday. Emma McIntyre at David Zwirner Tribeca: McIntyre’s new paintings and works on paper combine oil and oxidized iron, displaying her mastery of balancing control and spontaneity. 6. MoMA PS1 + Printed Matter’s New York Art Book Fair Sep. 24–27 | 22-25 Jackson Ave | Long Island City, Queens It’s an ideal time to get yourself to MoMA PS1 . The museum is opening a new show of Teresa Margolles on September 24th, while Precious Okoyomon ’s living installation is still on view in the courtyard. Meanwhile, Printed Matter’s New York Art Book Fair takes place over the weekend. The beloved annual event returns with its plethora of books, zines, and other printed wares from independent publishers and small presses. You can buy tickets for opening night on Thursday, September 24th, from 7 to 10 p.m., or for a visit throughout the weekend (the fair runs through Sunday). 7. New Museum 235 Bowery | Lower East Side The New Museum kicks off its fall season on September 24th with a full slate of new exhibitions. Leading the lineup is “ Arthur Jafa : I Am Tony,” the first U.S. museum survey of the esteemed artist, taking over two floors of the museum with new pieces alongside signature works like Love is the Message, The Message is Death (2016) and The White Album (2019). Alongside it is “ Diego Marcon : Arrivederci, Piggies!,” marking the artist’s New York solo museum debut, and the group show “The Bowery: Devil’s Mile” reflecting on four centuries of art and visual culture of the mile-long thoroughfare where the museum is located. 8. Amant 315 Maujer St | East Williamsburg, Brooklyn If you live in Brooklyn or you’re eager for an adventurous outing in the borough, I recommend a trip to East Williamsburg art foundation Amant. Two exhibitions have just opened: “Sentient Earth” is a group show bringing together artists tapping into the earth as a living, thinking being. Meanwhile, Matthew Lutz-Kinoy takes over another part of the space with “ The Mud Room: Itinerant Artists, Folk Spectacles, and Painted Walls ,” which presents a wonderfully theatrical ceramic studio. While there, check out Zoli , Amant’s restaurant next door, which boasts great design, an excitingly unusual menu, and Pierre Huyghe aquariums behind the bar. And a couple of blocks away, pop by Carvalho —the gallery is showing a two-artist show of paintings by Alicja Biała and textile sculptures by Diana Orving . 9. ICP 84 Ludlow St | Lower East Side If you need a break from fairs and galleries, head downtown to the photography institution ICP to catch the final weeks of two distinct and intriguing shows. “ Yves Saint Laurent and Photography” traces the four-decade relationship between the designer and the camera, with works by Richard Avedon , Irving Penn , and many more illustrious names. “Photobooks USA 2000–25” gathers more than 50 photo books from the last 25 years that trace salient themes and issues of American life, including race, migration, and labor. On Thursdays, the museum hosts ICP Late Night and stays open until 8 p.m. with $5 admission. This week, on September 24th, photographer Landon Nordeman will be shooting Instax portraits outside on Ludlow and Broome Streets. 10. SPRING/BREAK Art Show Sep. 24–28 | 555 West 57th Street | Hell’s Kitchen The free-wheeling art fair SPRING/BREAK is taking place this year in midtown at the former offices of CBS News, with more than 120 presentations organized by independent curators and artists. Revolving around the theme of “Hide n Seek,” early highlights include a show inspired by making art with kids, curated by Todd Bienvenu and Hannah Rowan, and featuring works by artists like Julie Curtiss and Katherine Bradford , a video work by Half Gallery founder Bill Powers, a presentation of sculptures by Stuart Lantry curated by Shona McAndrew , and a presentation exploring the perils of AI on writing, co-curated by novelist Jennifer Egan.

title: These Collectors Turned Family Tragedy into a Legacy of Supporting Artists and Cancer Patients
summary: Susan and Michael Hort are among New York’s most prolific collectors of emerging art. Over the decades, they’ve taken risks on countless artists, Marlene Dumas and Cindy Sherman among them. In the New York art world, the couple is synonymous with their Tribeca home, filled with wall-to-wall art by blue-chip names and little-known artists alike. But before the Horts were fixtures of the city’s gallery circuit, they were the parents of an art-loving daughter, Rema Hort Mann. On Saturdays, Rema would regularly pull her parents around the city to exhibitions, an entourage of young artist friends in tow. “I remember saying to Michael, ‘Do you think we could have dinner alone on a Saturday night without Rema and her five friends?’” Susan Hort said with a laugh during a recent conversation. Rema died of stomach cancer in 1995 at 30. In the wake of her death, her parents resolved to honor her life and founded the Rema Hort Mann Fund , a nonprofit organization with a two-pronged mission of supporting both cancer patients and the emerging artists Rema so championed in life. “It was very important that Rema’s name stay alive,” Susan said, “and let something good come out of her death.” The fund quickly became a family affair. Their son Peter, one of the couple’s three surviving children, had become closely involved with the fund’s quality-of-life grants for cancer patients. Tragically, Peter, who was a lawyer and judge, died suddenly in 2022, at 51, of bile duct cancer. His wife, Jamie Cohen, stepped into his role. This year, the Rema Hort Mann Fund is marking its 30th anniversary with a gala on October 28, 2026. In this milestone year, the Horts have added a new, third grant to the fund: the Artists Living with Cancer Grant. The grant, which merges the fund’s two longstanding missions into one, was inspired by this year’s gala honoree, celebrated contemporary artist Jacolby Satterwhite , who has lived with cancer and its complications since he was 11 years old. The artist is the recipient of inaugural Artists Living with Cancer Grant for $25,000, jointly funded by Rema Hort Mann Fund and the Robert Rauschenberg Foundation. A memory-fueled mission The Rema Hort Mann Fund has centered its mission around two grants, the Peter Hort Quality of Life Grant and the Emerging Artist Grant. The Quality of Life Grant supports people in cancer treatment, covering things like childcare, phone bills, travel, and housing. Its primary mission is to ensure that cancer patients are not alone during treatments and to strengthen their emotional support networks and financial resources. The inspiration for this grant came from a friend of Rema’s who was battling brain cancer. The friend met the Horts for dinner and told them she was going to stop treatment. “Her boyfriend had just left her. Her parents lived in the Northwest. She wanted one last good summer,” recalled Susan. “That’s where the idea for the grants came in. Maybe if her parents had been able to visit her and she had this connection, she would have fought. It’s very hard to fight when you’re alone.” The grant, which has long been overseen by family friend and board member Dr. David Biro, offers unrestricted grants of up to $10,000 and has supported over 2,400 people battling cancer (recipients must be nominated by their hospital social worker). For this grant, it’s been important to the family for the fund to be fast-acting and responsive to immediate needs. “So people don’t have to wait,” said Susan. The fund’s other grant, the Emerging Artist Grant, offers no-strings grants to burgeoning talents. Each year, over 100 artists receive a nomination-only invitation from dozens of accomplished arts professionals. Following a competitive selection process, an independent jury awards 10 recipients $12,500 each. One artist receives an additional $2,500 in honor of Peter Hort. Last year’s recipients include Taína Cruz , Daniel Castro , and Aiza Ahmed , among others. For Susan and Michael Hort, the Emerging Artist Grants pay the greatest homage to Rema’s irrepressible passion for artists and her bohemian worldview. “She was amazing,” said Michael simply. “She loved artists. She was always hanging out with them. She was also brilliant,” added Susan. Nicole Eisenman , for instance, attended Rema’s wedding to her husband Billy Mann, taking photographs of the couple as a gift. Rema was a high-powered professional. She worked at a major accounting firm as a management consultant, then earned her master’s at The Wharton School—but she always maintained an independent streak. “She was definitely more of a hippie than they wanted,” Susan recalled of Rema’s corporate job. “At one point they said to her, ‘If you want to be taken seriously as a woman, you have to cut your hair.’ She came to me and said, ‘What do I do?’ I said, ‘You want to cut your hair?’ So she left, and she went and worked for HBO in its infancy.” These memories have fueled the couple’s drive to keep the fund a strong presence over the decades, sustaining it through auctions, year-end donations, and personal money during leaner years. “When we didn’t have quite enough money, my husband and I put in money to make sure the grants would be paid,” Susan noted. Meeting the moment This year’s new grant, the Artists Living with Cancer grant, merges the two longstanding pillars of the Rema Hort Mann Fund. The goal is to support artists so they can continue their practice while seeking treatment. The grant provides a one-time grant for selected visual artists suffering with cancer and living in the New York metropolitan area. As with much of the Horts’ charitable work, the inspiration came through personal connection. Susan had met Satterwhite years ago, at one of her own birthday parties, where he performed. “He had so much fun, he refused to charge me,” she recalled. Satterwhite is best known for sprawling, maximalist video and performance works that blend 3D animation, personal family ephemera, and live movement. His practice has been shown at institutions including the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney , and he was named to The Artsy Vanguard in 2019. Soon after the birthday party, Carole Server, a board member of the fund, who knew Satterwhite personally, told Susan Hort about the artist’s battle with cancer and envisioned a way for the fund to support artists in similar positions. “When she came to me, and I heard it, I said, ‘That’s perfect,’” Susan said. The grant “is more needed now than there ever was.” The Horts have a history of supporting art world figures amid health struggles, particularly those who are uninsured. When their friend, the iconic New York dealer Pat Hearn, was diagnosed with liver cancer in 1997, she was denied treatment coverage. The Horts participated in the memorable “Emergency Sale” of artworks donated by artist friends, dealers, and collectors alike. In the New York Times, critic Roberta Smith detailed Hearn’s insurance struggles and the sale, an article that led her insurer, Oxford, to reconsider the claims. Sadly, Hearn passed away in 2000, at the age of 45. The Horts believe artists’ need for health care support has only grown in the years since. “It’s more needed now than it ever was,” said Michael. “Health care is much more expensive and not only that, artists aren’t making as much.” Since the grant was announced, the couple has heard from countless artists. “Everybody’s struggling right now. I have artists who are very successful and say to me, ‘This is the first time this show didn’t sell out,’” said Susan. “So if the very successful artists are having that experience, you can imagine what’s happening to the younger, not-quite-as-established artists.” “I hope this grant creates a shift in the art world,” Satterwhite told the Art Newspaper earlier this year . “The art world can be very fickle and fleeting, but artists give their whole lives to their work. When serious illness interrupts that, there should be more space for care, dignity, and support." An art world legacy and its future Room for Demoiselle Two, 2019-2025 Jacolby Satterwhite Kadel Willborn Today, Susan and Michael’s art collection exceeds 5,000 works, spread across their Tribeca triplex and their New Jersey home. For decades, the couple has collected by a mantra of buying early and buying deep. They were collectors of blue-chip artists like Peter Doig long before the market caught on. They hold sometimes over a dozen works by a single artist. “If I have one piece by an artist, I’m not really collecting that artist,” Susan said of their approach. Now the couple is focusing on a new horizon—the future of the collection and the fund. “We realized we're getting older,” Susan said. The couple has begun handing day-to-day control to a new executive director, Elysia Borowy. Meanwhile, their daughter now sits on the board, and a growing bench of grandchildren have expressed interest in collecting art. The next chapter of the collection is already under construction. The Horts are opening a pavilion with the nonprofit arts space Art Omi in upstate New York in 2027. The family is committing to two rotating shows a year, in a space that Art Omi will fund and staff, sparing their children the financial costs of a private museum. In a full-circle moment, many of the artists the Horts collected in the early years of their careers are now donating work to this year’s gala benefit. Among them are Cristina BanBan , discovered in a small London gallery years before her market took off, Nicole Eisenman , whom the Horts began collecting in 1992, and Marlene Dumas. Every dollar raised by the gala will go directly to supporting artists and patients. The board covers the fund’s operating costs out of pocket. For the Horts, the continuation of the fund for another 30 years is self-evident in its purpose. “We see it continuing, because there’s still a need,” said Susan.

title: Time features Amy Sherald on the cover of its inaugural “Most Influential People in Art” issue.
summary: Amy Sherald is the cover subject of Time ’s newly launched Time 100 Art list, photographed by Tyler Mitchell , who is himself named to the list. Time editor-in-chief Sam Jacobs noted in his letter to readers that it has been 50 years since a living painter appeared solo on the magazine's cover, since Robert Rauschenberg appeared in November 1976 . He called the gap in attention to fine art’s influence part of the impetus for the inaugural list, which also recognizes collectors, museum leaders, gallerists, curators, and other figures shaping the field, “even more exciting to debut.” Time CEO Jessica Sibley said the list also recognizes people “ whose vision is expanding the possibilities of art and shaping the global conversation.” The issue includes an accompanying profile of Sherald by Time editor at large Belinda Luscombe, tracing the artist’s practice and the trajectory that led to her best-known work, the official portrait of Michelle Obama commissioned by the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery in 2018. Sherald described color as central to her method, noting that she paints every canvas red before painting over it in the gray tones that define her portraits: “I consider the red kind of like the blood behind the figures there,” she said. “Color is my natural language. Using my voice is only the third best way that I communicate.” The profile also traces her path to that commission, from a formative encounter with a painting by Bo Bartlett to the artist’s heart transplant at 39 and her artworks’ runaway auction prices, including The Bathers (2015), which sold for $4.26 million at Phillips in 2021. The profile also revisits Sherald’s decision last year to withdraw her touring survey “American Sublime” from the National Portrait Gallery after Smithsonian officials expressed reservations about exhibiting Trans Forming Liberty (2024), a painting featuring a trans woman. “‘American Sublime’ has its own narrative,” Sherald said. “Deviating from that narrative would be deviating from the core person of who I am and why the work exists in the world, and I just wasn’t willing to do that.” The show was subsequently picked up by the Baltimore Museum of Art, where it broke attendance records. The broader Time 100 Art list spans artists including Petra Collins , Simone Leigh , KAWS , JR , Banksy , David Hammons , Jenny Holzer , and El Anatsui ; collectors and patrons such as Alicia Keys, Swizz Beatz, Bernard Arnault, and Ronald Lauder; museum and institutional leaders including Max Hollein, Michael Govan, and Thelma Golden; and gallerists and market figures such as David Zwirner , Larry Gagosian , and Amy Cappellazzo. Time will host the inaugural Time 100 Impact Dinner: Leaders Shaping the Future of Art on October 5th in New York, with appearances from list honorees including Keys, Swizz Beatz, and Lauder.
